case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Congress authorized (and the Double Jeopardy Clause therefore permits) imposing cumulative sentences for a single course of conduct resulting in convictions under both 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)(1)(A) and 18 U.S.C. § 924(j).
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. V (Double Jeopardy Clause); 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)(1)(A); 18 U.S.C. § 924(j).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Barrett argues cumulative punishment is not authorized because § 924(c) is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j) when both are based on the same firearm use during the same predicate crime, so under double-jeopardy/statutory-construction principles (including the presumption against multiple punishments absent clear congressional intent) he cannot be sentenced for both; § 924(j) also lacks § 924(c)’s consecutive-sentencing directive, reinforcing that Congress did not intend stacking § 924(c) on top of § 924(j) for the same conduct.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States (in its merits briefing here) supports Barrett: it contends § 924(c)(1)(A) is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j), which triggers a presumption against cumulative punishments that is not rebutted by any clear statutory text or structure; in particular, Congress expressly authorizes cumulative punishments for some combinations in § 924(c) but did not include language authorizing cumulation between § 924(c)(1)(A) and § 924(j), so Barrett may not be cumulatively sentenced for both based on the same underlying conduct. (By contrast, the court-appointed amicus defending the judgment below argues cumulative punishment is permitted because Congress indicated intent through § 924(c)’s 'in addition to' framework/mandatory minimum scheme and related statutory history, and under cases like Missouri v. Hunter only one statute needs to clearly authorize additional punishment.)
key_precedents: Flowers v. Mississippi, 136 S. Ct. 2157 (2016) (Alito, J., dissenting) (GVR practice)
Garland v. Range, No. 23-374 (U.S.) (government brief cited for 'hold' practice)
Delligatti v. United States, No. 23-825 (U.S.) (pending, referenced)

John Roberts.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest contention is that §924(c)’s “in addition to” and consecutive-sentencing directives necessarily require a separate §924(c) term whenever §924(j) is proved, because (j) occurs “in the course of a violation of subsection (c).” But as Justice Thomas explains, that structural incorporation makes the (c) violation an element of (j) on these facts, triggering our Whalen/Blockburger presumption against multiple punishments absent a clear congressional statement. Justice Alito’s point reinforces the negative implication: Congress repeatedly spoke plainly about stacking within §924(c), yet §924(j) omits comparable “in addition to” or consecutive language and provides its own penalty scheme. A narrow disposition vacating the cumulative §924(c) sentence and remanding for resentencing respects precedent, avoids broad disruption to §924(c), and best preserves institutional legitimacy.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The respondent’s best point is that §924(j) requires a killing “in the course of a violation of subsection (c),” so §924(c)’s “in addition to” and consecutive-sentencing commands should automatically generate a separate, stacked §924(c) term. But that reading treats §924(c)’s general punishment machinery as silently doing work that Congress conspicuously did not do in §924(j): §924(j) sets out its own penalty scheme and omits any “in addition to” or consecutive directive, and—per Justice Alito’s point—Congress elsewhere in §924(c) showed it knows how to speak expressly when it intends cumulation. As the Chief Justice explains, when the (c) violation is an element of (j) on these facts, our multiple-punishments cases demand clear authorization to stack; the text and structure here instead point the other way, because importing automatic cumulation would put the provisions at cross-purposes by converting an incorporated element into an additional mandatory punishment without Congress saying so. Applying the statute Congress enacted, I see no basis to uphold the extra §924(c) sentence.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point is that §924(j) applies only when a killing occurs “in the course of a violation of subsection (c),” so one might say §924(c)’s “in addition to” and consecutive-sentencing machinery should automatically require an extra §924(c) term. But as the Chief Justice explains, when the §924(c) violation is a lesser-included component of §924(j) on these facts, our multiple-punishments cases require a clear congressional statement to authorize cumulation, and §924(j) contains none—especially given Congress’s repeated, explicit stacking directives elsewhere in §924(c). Justice Thomas’s structural point is decisive: incorporation of (c) as an element explains how (j) aggravates (c), not that Congress silently mandated two punishments for the same firearm use and predicate offense. Reading §924(c)’s general “in addition to” language to do that work would effect a major sentencing change by implication, something Congress does not “hide” in this way absent unmistakable text.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The respondent’s best point is that §924(c)’s “in addition to” and consecutive-sentencing language should attach whenever a defendant has, by definition, committed a “violation of subsection (c),” including when that violation is proved as an element of §924(j). But §924(j) is the more specific enactment for killings committed “in the course of a violation of subsection (c),” and Congress gave it its own penalty scheme while conspicuously omitting §924(c)’s consecutive directive—an omission I cannot treat as accidental or silently overridden. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, when §924(c) is a lesser-included component of §924(j) on these facts, Blockburger/Whalen require a clear statement to authorize cumulative punishment, and §924(j)’s text supplies none. Fidelity to the enacted text and structure therefore requires vacating the additional §924(c) sentence and remanding for resentencing.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The strongest respondent argument would be that §924(j) is a freestanding homicide offense and that §924(c)’s “in addition to” and consecutive-sentencing machinery should therefore still attach whenever the Government also charges (c). But that would make cumulative punishment turn on charging formalities rather than Congress’s offense design, and it runs headlong into the clear-statement rule for multiple punishments when one offense is a lesser-included of the other. As Justice Roberts emphasizes, Blockburger/Whalen supplies a presumption against stacking here because §924(j) applies only “in the course of a violation of subsection (c),” and §924(j)’s omission of §924(c)’s consecutive directive is a structural signal Congress did not authorize cumulation. I therefore remain persuaded that the better, administrable reading treats §924(j) as the aggravated form of the §924(c) offense for the same firearm use and predicate, barring an extra §924(c) sentence absent clearer congressional instruction.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Respondent’s strongest contention is that § 924(j) is a distinct offense in a distinct subsection, and that because it occurs “in the course of a violation of subsection (c),” § 924(c)’s “in addition to” and consecutive-sentencing machinery should still mandate a separate stacked term. But as Justice Thomas stresses, that same phrase makes a (c) violation an element of (j) on these facts, and under Whalen/Blockburger we do not presume cumulative punishment absent a clear statement. I agree with the Chief Justice that Congress’s omission of § 924(c)’s consecutive directive from § 924(j)—despite Congress’s demonstrated ability to speak plainly about stacking—counsels against inferring an extra punishment by implication. Separation-of-powers principles and the rule of lenity reinforce that we should not manufacture cumulative penalties the statute does not clearly prescribe.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Respondent’s strongest point is that § 924(j) requires a killing “in the course of a violation of subsection (c),” so § 924(c)’s “in addition to” and consecutive-sentencing directives should automatically carry over and mandate a separate stacked § 924(c) term. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, our multiple-punishments cases (Whalen/Blockburger) require a clear congressional statement to authorize cumulative punishment when one offense is a lesser-included component of the other on these facts, and § 924(j) conspicuously supplies its own penalty scheme while omitting § 924(c)’s consecutive command. Reading § 924(c)’s general “in addition to” language to do the stacking work here would create a structurally incongruous sentencing regime—turning an incorporated element into an implied extra sentence—without the express statutory authorization we typically demand, especially in sentencing-modification and punishment-allocation contexts. The better reading respects Congress’s enacted text and preserves coherence: punish under § 924(j) without imposing an additional § 924(c) sentence for the same firearm use and predicate crime absent unmistakable direction.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The respondent’s best argument is that § 924(c)’s “in addition to” and consecutive-sentencing commands necessarily require a separate § 924(c) sentence whenever the Government proves a § 924(j) killing “in the course of” a (c) violation. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Thomas explain, once (c) is a lesser-included offense of (j) on these facts, Blockburger/Whalen supplies a presumption against cumulative punishment that can be overcome only by a clear congressional statement—and § 924(j)’s text conspicuously omits § 924(c)’s stacking and consecutive directives while supplying its own penalty range. Reading § 924(c)’s general sentencing machinery to do the work § 924(j) does not do would allow implication to substitute for the unmistakable authorization our multiple-punishments cases demand. I therefore remain persuaded the additional § 924(c) sentence cannot stand and the proper course is to vacate and remand for resentencing.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The respondent’s best contention—that §924(j)’s reference to conduct “in the course of a violation of subsection (c)” silently imports §924(c)’s consecutive-sentencing mandate and thereby requires stacking—asks us to supply a cumulation rule Congress did not enact in §924(j)’s own penalty provision. As Justice Thomas and Justice Kagan emphasize, Congress placed §924(j) in a separate subsection, provided an independent sentencing range, and omitted §924(c)’s consecutive directive; that structural and textual omission is powerful evidence that §924(c)’s machinery does not automatically carry over. Even assuming arguendo the Double Jeopardy “same offense” premise, the Whalen/Blockburger clear-statement requirement for multiple punishments (highlighted by the Chief Justice) is not satisfied by §924(c)’s general “in addition to” language, which is aimed at the predicate offense rather than §924(j). Fidelity to the statutory command, not policy intuitions about severity, counsels vacating the extra §924(c) sentence when both counts rest on the same firearm use and predicate.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under our multiple-punishments cases, the Double Jeopardy Clause permits cumulative sentences only when Congress clearly authorizes them; absent such clarity, Blockburger operates as a presumption against stacking punishments where one offense is a lesser-included of the other. Here, on the facts presented—a single firearm use during the same predicate crime resulting in convictions under both § 924(c)(1)(A) and § 924(j)—§ 924(c) is best understood as a lesser-included component of § 924(j), triggering that presumption. Neither the text nor structure of § 924(j) supplies the clear indication necessary to rebut it, particularly given Congress’s demonstrated ability elsewhere in § 924(c) to speak expressly when it intends cumulative punishment. A narrow disposition vacating the cumulative sentencing and remanding for resentencing resolves the case without unsettling broader aspects of § 924(c)’s regime, serving institutional legitimacy and adherence to precedent.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Double Jeopardy question here reduces to what Congress actually authorized, and the statutory text and structure do not authorize cumulative punishment for the same firearm use supporting both §924(c)(1)(A) and §924(j). Section 924(j) expressly applies only “in the course of a violation of subsection (c),” which incorporates a (c) violation as a necessary component of (j) and thus triggers the traditional presumption against stacking absent clear authorization. Reading the provisions harmoniously, Congress knew how to require additional or consecutive punishment in §924(c) when it wished, yet §924(j) contains no “in addition to” or consecutive-sentencing command for a separate §924(c) term—an omission that, under the negative-implication canon, is best understood as withholding authorization for cumulation. Because there is no clear textual statement overcoming that structural inference, imposing both sentences for the same course of conduct exceeds what the statute Congress enacted permits.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The enacted text and structure show that Congress knew how to authorize cumulative punishments in clear terms, as § 924(c)(1)(A) expressly mandates punishment “in addition to” the predicate crime and elsewhere in § 924(c) speaks with specificity about stacking, but § 924(j) contains no parallel cumulation or consecutive-sentencing command when the same firearm use during the same predicate offense results in death. Because § 924(c) is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j) on these facts, the Blockburger presumption against multiple punishments applies and is not rebutted by any clear statement; I would not infer such a major sentencing consequence from general “in addition to” language aimed at the predicate offense rather than at § 924(j) itself. Reading the statutes to permit double punishment here would create a substantial, systemwide increase in sentencing exposure for a single course of conduct—exactly the sort of fundamental change Congress does not “hide” in an ancillary or indirectly related provision. The better reading, consistent with Congress’s targeted approach to serious firearm violence, is that § 924(j) supplies the punishment for the death-resulting conduct and does not silently authorize an extra § 924(c) sentence for the same act.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Double Jeopardy question here reduces to statutory authorization: if § 924(c)(1)(A) is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j) when both rest on the same firearm use during the same predicate crime, cumulative punishment requires a clear congressional statement. Nothing in § 924(j)’s text authorizes stacking a separate § 924(c) sentence on top of a § 924(j) sentence for the same conduct, and Congress’s omission of § 924(c)’s consecutive-sentencing command from § 924(j) is a strong textual signal that courts should not supply that added punishment by implication. Nor does § 924(c)’s general “in addition to” framework clearly speak to cumulation with § 924(j) specifically, especially given that Congress elsewhere knows how to expressly authorize cumulative punishments when it wishes to do so. Because the enacted text and structure do not clearly permit two punishments for this single course of conduct, one of the sentences must be vacated.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Read in its ordinary statutory context, §924(j) does not create a free-standing add-on penalty to be stacked atop §924(c) for the very same firearm use; it instead incorporates a §924(c) violation as an element and then adds the homicide requirement, making §924(c) a lesser-included offense on these facts. Under the anti-multiplicity presumption reflected in Blockburger/Whalen, cumulative punishment requires a clear congressional indication, and the statute’s structure cuts the other way: Congress knew how to authorize cumulation expressly within §924(c)’s scheme, yet §924(j) lacks §924(c)’s consecutive-sentencing directive and contains no comparably clear instruction to impose both punishments for one course of conduct. Accepting a stacking rule here would make the inquiry turn on formal charging choices rather than the single criminal episode Congress addressed—an administrable, non-trifling reading treats §924(j) as the aggravated form of the same §924(c) offense, not an additional one. Because Congress has not clearly authorized cumulative sentences for §924(c) and §924(j) based on the same predicate and firearm use, the Double Jeopardy Clause bars them.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Double Jeopardy Clause permits cumulative punishment only when Congress clearly authorizes it, and our cases treat Blockburger as a tool for discerning that intent. Here, § 924(j) incorporates the elements of § 924(c)(1)(A) (a § 924(c) violation plus a killing in the course of it), making § 924(c) a lesser-included offense and triggering the presumption against multiple punishments for the same conduct. Nothing in the plain text of § 924(j) clearly rebuts that presumption—especially given that Congress elsewhere in § 924(c) spoke expressly when it wanted stacking and § 924(j) itself omits § 924(c)’s consecutive-sentencing command. Absent a clear statement authorizing cumulation, separation-of-powers principles and the rule of lenity counsel that courts may not impose two punishments for the same firearm use and predicate crime.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The starting point is the enacted text and Congress’s sentencing design: Section 924(j) punishes a firearm-caused death "in the course of a violation of subsection (c)," which makes a same-conduct 924(c)(1)(A) conviction a lesser-included component of the 924(j) offense. Under this Court’s multiple-punishments cases, that overlap triggers the presumption against cumulative punishment absent clear congressional authorization, and nothing in § 924(j)’s text or structure expressly authorizes stacking an additional § 924(c) term on top of the § 924(j) sentence for the same firearm use and predicate crime. Reading § 924(c)’s consecutive-sentencing directive to mandate cumulation here would create an incongruous sentencing scheme in which Congress silently required extra, mandatory consecutive time on top of the homicide offense even though § 924(j) omits § 924(c)’s consecutive command and provides its own penalty range, and I would not displace Congress’s chosen categories without a clear statement. Given finality concerns and the rule that cumulative punishment must be clearly authorized by Congress, the Double Jeopardy Clause bars the extra § 924(c) punishment on these facts.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Double Jeopardy Clause’s multiple-punishments inquiry turns on what Congress authorized, and our cases use Blockburger as a rule of statutory construction to identify whether Congress meant two convictions to carry cumulative sentences. Here, § 924(c)(1)(A) is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j) when both convictions rest on the same firearm use during the same predicate crime, which triggers the presumption against cumulative punishment absent a clear statement of contrary intent. Nothing in § 924(j)’s text clearly authorizes stacking an additional § 924(c) sentence on top of the § 924(j) punishment for the same conduct, and § 924(j)’s omission of § 924(c)’s consecutive-sentencing directive reinforces that Congress did not make that authorization. Under our doctrine, “imprecise” inferences from § 924(c)’s general “in addition to” framework cannot overcome the absence of a clear congressional authorization for cumulative sentences in this specific § 924(c)/§ 924(j) pairing.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Starting with the enacted text and structure, §924(j) is set out as a separate subsection from §924(c) and—unlike provisions where Congress "groups" penalties and joins them with "and"—nothing in §924(j) textually links its punishment to §924(c)’s mandatory minimum and consecutive-sentencing machinery. Congress also "plainly chose a different approach" in §924(j): it generally provides sentencing flexibility (e.g., terms up to life or death) rather than importing §924(c)’s consecutive mandate, which is strong structural evidence that Congress did not authorize automatic stacking of a §924(c)(1)(A) sentence on top of a §924(j) sentence for the same firearm use during the same predicate crime. Assuming arguendo that §924(c) is a lesser-included offense of §924(j) on these facts, that Double Jeopardy premise triggers the presumption against cumulative punishments, and the statute’s architecture supplies no clear statement rebutting it. Under fidelity to the statutory command—not policy intuition about harshness—cumulative sentences are not authorized here and thus may not be imposed.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Double Jeopardy Clause permits imposing cumulative sentences when a defendant is convicted under both 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)(1)(A) and § 924(j) for the same firearm use during the same predicate crime (here, a Hobbs Act robbery resulting in death).
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. V (Double Jeopardy Clause) and 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)(1)(A) and § 924(j).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Barrett argues that § 924(c) is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j) when both are predicated on the same underlying crime and the same firearm use, so cumulative punishment is presumed not intended; because Congress did not clearly authorize stacking § 924(c) and § 924(j) punishments for the same conduct (unlike other places where Congress expressly authorizes cumulative penalties), imposing two sentences violates Double Jeopardy/legislative-intent limits on multiple punishments.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States (in its merits briefing here) supports Barrett: it contends § 924(c)(1)(A) is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j), triggering a presumption against cumulative punishment absent a clear statement from Congress; Congress expressly authorized cumulative punishments in some contexts within § 924(c) but did not include language authorizing cumulative sentencing for a § 924(j) conviction plus a separate § 924(c) conviction based on the same conduct, so stacking is not permitted.
key_precedents: Flowers v. Mississippi, 136 S. Ct. 2157 (2016) (Alito, J., dissenting) (cited re GVR practice)
Delligatti v. United States, No. 23-825 (pending, referenced)
Garland v. Range, No. 23-374 (referenced in briefing for holding/GVR practice)

John Roberts.reasoning: The narrow, dispositive question is whether Congress clearly authorized cumulative punishment when the same firearm use in the same predicate robbery supports both a § 924(c)(1)(A) conviction and a § 924(j) conviction. Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett correctly emphasize that § 924(j) incorporates “a violation of subsection (c)” as an element and then aggravates it when death results, making § 924(c) a lesser-included offense on these facts and triggering the Blockburger/Whalen presumption against multiple punishments absent a clear statement. The Government’s strongest contention—that § 924(c)’s “in addition to” and consecutive-sentence provisions evidence a general pro-stacking policy—does not answer the specific cumulation question here, because those clauses plainly address stacking with the predicate offense, not stacking § 924(c) on top of § 924(j) for the very same § 924(c) conduct. As Justice Alito notes, allowing cumulation based on that general policy would effectively let charging choices, rather than statutory text, drive substantial sentencing disparities, which our multiple-punishments cases do not permit.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Government’s best point is that § 924(c) reflects an aggressive anti-stacking policy—its “in addition to” and consecutive-sentence commands show Congress wanted cumulative punishment in firearm cases. But as Chief Justice Roberts explains, those directives speak to stacking § 924(c) on top of the predicate offense (and other specified punishments), not stacking § 924(c) on top of § 924(j) when § 924(j) already makes “a violation of subsection (c)” an element of the aggravated offense. On these facts, § 924(c)(1)(A) is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j), so Whalen/Blockburger’s presumption against multiple punishments applies absent a clear statement—and § 924(j)’s silence is not such a statement. Respecting Congress’ enacted text means we cannot treat general pro-cumulation language elsewhere as authorization to impose an extra § 924(c) sentence for the very same § 924(c) conduct.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Government’s best argument—that § 924(c)’s “in addition to” and consecutive-sentencing language reflects a broad pro-cumulation policy—cannot do the work it needs to do here because those clauses speak to stacking § 924(c) on top of the predicate offense, not on top of an aggravated offense (§ 924(j)) that itself requires “a violation of subsection (c)” as an element. As the Chief Justice notes, when Congress intends cumulative punishments for the same conduct it knows how to say so clearly, and § 924(j)’s silence is not the clear authorization Whalen/Blockburger require to overcome the presumption against multiple punishments for a lesser-included offense. Allowing stacking here would make sentence length turn on charging decisions rather than statutory meaning, producing the sort of arbitrary disparities that confirm the textual reading. Justice Kagan’s point that § 924(j) subsumes the § 924(c) elements on these facts reinforces that § 924(c) is lesser-included and not separately punishable absent an unmistakable statement.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Government’s strongest point remains that §924(c)’s “in addition to” language and §924(c)(1)(D)(ii)’s consecutive-sentencing command reflect a broad pro-stacking policy. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, that policy is expressed with precision as to stacking §924(c) punishment on top of the predicate offense; it does not clearly authorize an additional §924(c) sentence on top of §924(j) when §924(j) itself makes “a violation of subsection (c)” an element. Under Whalen/Blockburger, that incorporation makes §924(c) a lesser-included offense on these facts and triggers the presumption against multiple punishments absent a clear statement, which §924(j) lacks. Given the dramatic consecutive sentencing consequences, inferring cumulation from silence would effectively let charging choices, not Congress’s clear command, drive added punishment—an outcome our multiple-punishments cases do not tolerate.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Government’s best point—that §924(j) is a freestanding homicide offense with its own penalties and so can sit atop a separate §924(c) term—still runs headlong into the text Congress chose: §924(j) applies only when death is caused “in the course of a violation of subsection (c),” which necessarily makes §924(c) a lesser-included offense on these facts and triggers the Whalen/Blockburger presumption against cumulative punishments absent a clear statement. As Chief Justice Roberts stresses, when Congress wants stacking it says so unmistakably (“in addition to” and mandatory consecutiveness) in §924(c); §924(j) contains no comparable directive authorizing an extra §924(c) sentence for the same firearm use. Accepting the Government’s view would allow massive sentencing consequences to hinge on a charging choice—a kind of “trifle” inconsistent with Congress’s calibrated enhancement scheme and our rule-like approach in severe-penalty contexts. The better reading confines punishment to §924(j) alone here, leaving prosecutors free to charge §924(c) only where §924(j) is not proved.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Government’s best point is that § 924(c)’s “in addition to” and consecutive-sentencing provisions reflect a general anti-firearm-violence policy favoring cumulation. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, that language addresses punishment in addition to the predicate offense, not a second punishment for the very same § 924(c) conduct once § 924(j) already makes “a violation of subsection (c)” an element. Under Blockburger/Whalen, § 924(c) is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j) on these facts, so the Double Jeopardy Clause’s multiple-punishments rule demands a clear statement before we allow stacking—and § 924(j) supplies none. Accepting the Government’s broader inference would invite precisely the sort of circumvention risk the Clause guards against, turning charging decisions into a mechanism for successive bites at the same offense.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Government’s best argument is that § 924(j) is a freestanding homicide offense and that § 924(c)’s broader “in addition to” and consecutive-sentence provisions reflect a general congressional pro-stacking policy. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 924(j) is textually pegged to “a violation of subsection (c),” so when both counts rest on the same firearm use in the same predicate crime, § 924(c) is a lesser-included offense and Whalen/Blockburger supply a presumption against cumulative punishments absent a clear statement. Congress knows how to authorize stacking explicitly in § 924(c); § 924(j) contains no comparable clear authorization to add a second § 924(c) sentence on top of the § 924(j) sentence for the same conduct, and we should not infer a dramatically harsher regime from silence. Allowing cumulation here would make sentencing turn heavily on charging choices rather than the statutory elements Congress enacted, which is an administrability and fairness problem our multiple-punishments cases are designed to prevent.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Government’s strongest contention—that §924(j) is a freestanding homicide offense for which Congress implicitly intended an additional, consecutive §924(c) sentence—cannot overcome the statutes’ text and our multiple-punishments framework. As Justice Kagan and the Chief explain, §924(j) applies only when death is caused “in the course of a violation of subsection (c),” which makes the §924(c) violation an element and renders §924(c) a lesser-included offense on these facts, triggering the Blockburger/Whalen presumption against cumulation absent a clear statement. The “in addition to” and consecutive-sentence language in §924(c) speaks to punishment layered on the predicate offense, not to stacking a separate §924(c) sentence atop §924(j) for the same §924(c) conduct. Given Congress’s demonstrated ability to speak clearly when it wants cumulation, §924(j)’s silence is dispositive against inferring authorization for duplicative punishment.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Government’s strongest point—that § 924(j) is a distinct homicide offense and that § 924(c)’s pro-stacking policy should carry over—still fails the clear-statement requirement in the multiple-punishments context. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 924(j) is explicitly predicated on “a violation of subsection (c),” so when both counts rest on the same gun use during the same predicate crime, § 924(c) functions as a lesser-included offense and Whalen/Blockburger presumptively bar cumulative punishment absent unmistakable authorization. The fact that Congress wrote “in addition to” and consecutive-sentence commands in § 924(c) when it wanted stacking underscores that § 924(j)’s silence cannot be treated as permission to impose an extra mandatory term. Allowing stacking here would make extreme sentencing exposure turn on charging discretion rather than on any additional jury-found conduct beyond what § 924(j) already captures, undermining procedural fairness and uniformity.

John Roberts.reasoning: The precise question is whether Congress clearly authorized cumulative punishments when the same firearm use in the same Hobbs Act robbery supports convictions under both § 924(c)(1)(A) and § 924(j). Reading the statutes in context, § 924(j) incorporates a § 924(c) violation and adds the “death results” element, making § 924(c) a lesser-included offense on these facts and triggering the presumption against multiple punishments absent a clear statement. Unlike § 924(c)(1)(A)’s express “in addition to” language for the predicate crime, § 924(j) contains no comparably plain authorization to stack an additional § 924(c) sentence on top of a § 924(j) sentence for the same conduct. Under the Double Jeopardy Clause’s multiple-punishments inquiry—which turns on legislative intent—one of the two sentences must be vacated.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Double Jeopardy question in a single prosecution turns on Congress’ authorization of cumulative punishment, and we must apply the statutes as written rather than manufacture permission to stack sentences. On their face, § 924(j) incorporates a § 924(c) violation as an element (use of a firearm “in the course of a violation of subsection (c)”) and then adds the death-resulting requirement, making § 924(c)(1)(A) a lesser-included offense on these facts (the same firearm use during the same Hobbs Act robbery). Unlike provisions where Congress expressly commands cumulative punishment, nothing in § 924(j) clearly authorizes an additional, separate § 924(c) sentence for the same conduct, so the presumption against multiple punishments applies and one conviction must be vacated. Adhering to Congress’ textual framework, we cannot treat silence as a clear statement permitting two punishments for the same § 924(c) conduct simply because the Government charged both counts.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Reading the statutes as Congress wrote them, § 924(j) expressly incorporates a violation of § 924(c) and then adds the additional requirement that the firearm use cause death; in ordinary terms, that makes § 924(c) a lesser-included offense of § 924(j) when both counts rest on the same Hobbs Act robbery and the same firearm use. Under the Court’s multiple-punishments framework, that triggers the presumption against cumulative punishment unless Congress clearly indicated otherwise, and nothing in the text of § 924(j) (or § 924(c)(1)(A)) clearly authorizes stacking an additional § 924(c) sentence on top of a § 924(j) sentence for the very same conduct. It is not a court’s role to manufacture cumulative penalties from silence, particularly where doing so would create arbitrary sentencing disparities depending on charging choices rather than on real-world differences in criminal conduct. Because Congress did not speak with the clarity it has used elsewhere when it wants cumulative punishment, the Double Jeopardy Clause bars imposing both sentences here.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Double Jeopardy Clause bars multiple punishments for the same offense unless Congress clearly authorizes them, and our cases treat that inquiry as one of legislative intent. Here, §924(j) expressly incorporates §924(c) as its core conduct element (a death caused “through the use of a firearm” “in the course of a violation of subsection (c)”), making §924(c)(1)(A) a lesser-included offense of §924(j) when both counts rest on the same firearm use during the same Hobbs Act robbery. Nothing in §924(j)’s text supplies the kind of clear statement Congress has used elsewhere in §924(c) to mandate additional cumulative punishment, and reading both provisions to require consecutive stacking would dramatically increase mandatory exposure without an explicit congressional directive. Given that absence of clear authorization, the presumption against cumulative punishment controls and the two sentences for the same conduct cannot both stand.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Start with text and structure: §924(j) punishes causing death “in the course of a violation of subsection (c),” so a valid §924(j) conviction necessarily includes every element of a §924(c)(1)(A) offense, making §924(c) a lesser-included offense on these facts (the same firearm use during the same Hobbs Act robbery). Under the multiple-punishments strand of Double Jeopardy, that triggers the Blockburger/Whalen presumption against cumulative sentences unless Congress clearly says otherwise. Nothing in §924(j) or the surrounding §924(c) penalty scheme supplies that clear authorization—unlike other parts of §924(c) where Congress expressly directs cumulation—so the Government’s (and the court’s) stacking would impose severe, extra punishment without a statutory limiting principle. Consistent with avoiding outcomes turning on “trifles,” the availability of two sentences should not hinge on charging choices when the statutes’ elements show Congress designed §924(j) as the aggravated form of §924(c) for the same gun use resulting in death.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Double Jeopardy Clause forbids being twice put in jeopardy “for the same offense,” and under Blockburger two statutes define the same offense when one contains no element the other does not. Here, when both counts rest on the same Hobbs Act robbery and the same firearm use, § 924(c)(1)(A) is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j): § 924(j) necessarily incorporates the § 924(c) elements and adds only the death-resulting (and mens rea) requirements. Because that triggers the presumption against cumulative punishments for the same offense, the only question is whether Congress clearly authorized stacking—and § 924(c)’s express “in addition to” language for predicate crimes, coupled with its silence as to cumulative punishment with § 924(j), supplies no clear statement overcoming that presumption. Allowing both sentences would invite the very sort of charge-stacking that lets the government obtain in substance what the Constitution forbids in form: multiple punishments for the same offense.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: This case is about multiple punishments in a single proceeding, which turns on Congress’s intent: the Double Jeopardy Clause forbids a sentencing court from imposing greater punishment than the legislature authorized. Here, § 924(c)(1)(A) functions as a lesser-included offense of § 924(j) when both rest on the same firearm use during the same Hobbs Act robbery, so the Blockburger presumption against cumulative punishment applies. Looking to statutory structure, Congress knows how to clearly authorize stacking within § 924(c), but it did not clearly provide that a defendant may receive separate, cumulative sentences under both § 924(c) and § 924(j) for the same conduct. Respecting Congress’s primacy in setting sentencing policy, the Court should not infer cumulative punishment absent a clear statement, so imposing both sentences here violates the multiple-punishments limitation.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Double Jeopardy Clause’s “same offence” inquiry, in the multiple-punishments setting, turns on what Congress authorized: the Constitution bars a sentencing court from imposing greater punishment than the legislature intended. Here, § 924(j) incorporates all the elements of § 924(c)(1)(A) (same firearm use during the same predicate Hobbs Act robbery) and adds the death-resulting element, so § 924(c) is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j) and a presumption arises that Congress did not intend cumulative punishment absent a clear statement. Nothing in § 924’s text clearly authorizes stacking a separate § 924(c) sentence on top of a § 924(j) sentence for the same firearm use in the same predicate crime, especially given that Congress did expressly authorize cumulative punishment in other parts of § 924(c) but not here. Applying the Court’s holding-focused framework, that absence of a clear authorization means the cumulative sentences exceed what Congress prescribed and therefore violate the Double Jeopardy Clause’s multiple-punishments limit.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: In the multiple-punishments context, the Double Jeopardy Clause functions as a limit on sentencing courts: they may not impose greater cumulative punishment than Congress clearly authorized. Here, § 924(j) expressly incorporates “a violation of subsection (c),” so under Blockburger § 924(c)(1)(A) is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j) when both counts rest on the same Hobbs Act robbery and the same firearm use resulting in death. Absent a clear statement that Congress intended stacking in this precise situation—especially given that Congress has been explicit elsewhere in § 924(c) when it wants cumulative penalties—procedural fairness and the practical consequences for sentencing require treating the duplicative § 924(c) sentence as unauthorized. The proper course is to vacate the cumulative punishment and allow only the § 924(j) sentence for the single firearm episode tied to the single predicate crime.
